subject: Post-call: SDK & structured-output reliability for LumenHealth integration
messages:
From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>

Cc: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 27 Jun 2027 15:20:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call: SDK & structured-output reliability for LumenHealth integration

Hi Alice —

Thanks again for taking the product/tech call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment before the engineering deep-dive. Appreciate a quick confirm or any edits.

Call notes / decisions:
- Integration mode: Dedicated capacity (pilot) to start for PHI-adjacent telemetry.
- Auth: OAuth2 service accounts + short-lived tokens; token scopes scoped per-route (generate-only embedding, inference, rerank).
- Routing: primary region us-west; fallback to us-east if capacity constrained.
- SDK: you will use the Redwood JS SDK (server-side) for initial integration; client calls should go through your backend proxy.
- Embeddings / reranker: compute LumenHealth embeddings in an offline pipeline and store in your vector DB; reranking on read path using top-K + re-score.
- Structured output: we agreed on a JSON-first contract for downstream systems; Redwood will validate model outputs against a schema and provide deterministic fallback when validation fails.

Open technical recommendations (we attached drafts):
1) Constrained decoding + strong validation: prefer constrained decoding (token whitelists / grammar-guided sampling) for critical fields + server-side JSON schema validation as a safety net.
2) Idempotent retries: every request should include a client-generated idempotency_key; retries should be retried safely with deduplication on our side.
3) Retry/backoff pattern: recommend exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 retries for generation calls; for schema-validation failures, attempt a single automatic correction pass (see playbook) before surfacing to your service.
4) Fallback behavior: deterministic fallback should return a strict, minimal schema-compliant payload (e.g., empty arrays / default enum values) plus a `validation_status` field so downstream consumers can detect degraded results.

Action items / owners:
- Marcus (me): send SDK quickstart + schema draft (attached) — DONE (see attachments).
- Alice: confirm schema fields and mark any PHI-sensitive attributes that need redaction before sending to Redwood.
- Vanessa: schedule a 90-minute technical deep-dive with your infra + security teams (propose times).

Proposed times for deep-dive (PST): Tue 6/29 10–11:30am, Wed 6/30 8–9:30am. Tell us which works and we’ll send calendar invites.

Attachments: redwood_sdk_quickstart.pdf (server-side setup, auth examples), lumen_schema_draft.json (first pass of POI/events schema).

Thanks — looking forward to moving to pilot.

—

Hi Alice / Marcus —

Short technical follow-up on the specific items Alice raised. I’ll walk through recommended patterns we use in pilots and why they balance reliability vs. recall.

1) Constrained decoding vs recall:
- Constrained decoding should be used only for syntactic/semantic fields where correctness is critical (e.g., ICD codes, structured enums, ISO timestamps, IDs). For free-text clinical summaries we recommend permissive decoding and separate extraction pipelines.
- For mixed fields, use a two-stage approach: permissive generation -> extraction + constrained parser. This preserves recall in the free-text while producing structured tokens for downstream consumers.

2) Automatic correction pass:
- Pattern: run generation -> server-side JSON schema validation. If validation fails and failures are minor (missing optional keys, wrong enum casing, trailing commas), auto-correct locally using a deterministic sanitizer (fix casing, fill defaults).
- If failures are structural (missing required nested objects, malformed arrays), attempt a single constrained re-generation with the same prompt but a short instruction to "return strictly valid JSON matching schema v2" and include the previous output as context. Limit this to 1 retry to avoid instability.
- We log both attempts and surface a `validation_status` (ok | corrected | failed) and `validation_errors` array in the response.

3) Embeddings lifecycle for 12M documents:
- Bulk initial compute (batch jobs, GPUs). For ongoing updates: incremental on write is generally best for freshness; schedule a nightly batch reindex for expensive re-embeds if you perform model upgrades or re-quantization.
- Store vectors in your managed vector DB with versioning metadata (embedding_model:v1). Redwood can provide an embeddings migration script if you decide to change models.

4) Token rotation / KMS / retention:
- Token rotation cadence: recommend rotating service-account keys every 90 days and short-lived access tokens for inference (TTL < 1h).
- KMS: we support AWS KMS and Google Cloud KMS for key wrapping.
- Retention: KV cache is configurable; default short-term cache is 24 hours. Logs for audit can be retained per your compliance tier — we have an enterprise setting for 7+ years if needed.

Operational recommendations (practical):
- Idempotency: require client-supplied idempotency_key for generation calls; we dedupe within 24 hours.
- Retry: exponential backoff with full jitter (base 200ms, factor 2, max 2500ms), max_attempts=3 for network/timeout errors. For model validation failures use the single auto-correct attempt described above.

I attached a short playbook that illustrates the validation flow and sample SDK config (structured_output_validation_playbook.pdf).

If everyone is good with Tuesday 6/29 10am PST, I’ll send an invite and include our infra/security leads.

—
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Solutions Engineering | Redwood Inference
